definition: Uniform Resource Locator: the address of a resource on the web. It is made of a scheme (such as https), a host name, an optional port, a path and an optional query string and fragment.
example: In https://shop.example.com/cart?id=4 the scheme is https, the host is shop.example.com, the path is /cart and the query is id=4.

definition: The human-readable name of a machine or service, such as shop.example.com. DNS translates it into an IP address before a connection can be opened.
example: api.example.com and www.example.com are two hostnames under the domain example.com.

definition: The network-layer protocol that carries packets from a source address to a destination address across interconnected networks. TCP, UDP and QUIC all run on top of it.
example: A browser's TCP segments to a web server travel inside IP packets addressed to the server's IP address.

definition: A small unit of data sent across a network, with a header (addresses and control information) and a payload. Large messages are split into many packets.
example: A 1,500-byte Ethernet packet can carry about 1,460 bytes of TCP data.

definition: A 16-bit number (0 to 65,535) that, together with an IP address, identifies which program on a host a connection or datagram is for. Well-known services have standard ports.
example: HTTPS uses TCP port 443, plain HTTP uses port 80 and DNS uses port 53.

definition: One step along a path from one machine or component to the next, for example browser to CDN edge, or load balancer to app server. Every network hop adds some latency and is another place that can fail.
example: Browser → CDN → load balancer → app server is three hops.

definition: Sending a message and waiting for the reply to come back. Many network operations, such as handshakes, cost a whole number of round trips, each taking one round-trip time (RTT).
example: A TCP handshake costs one round trip: SYN out, SYN-ACK back.

definition: The time from a client starting a request until the first byte of the response arrives. It includes DNS, connection set-up, network travel and server processing.
example: A cold HTTPS request with 80 ms RTT and 20 ms of server time has a TTFB of about 260 ms.

definition: The time a signal takes to travel a physical distance, set by the speed of the signal in the medium. In optical fibre light travels at roughly 200,000 km/s, so distance puts a hard floor under latency.
example: 5,900 km of fibre takes about 30 ms one way, so a round trip cannot be faster than about 60 ms.

definition: A thin glass strand that carries data as pulses of light. Light in fibre travels at about two-thirds of its vacuum speed, roughly 200,000 km/s, which is why long-distance latency cannot be engineered away.
The shortest path between two points on the Earth's surface. Real cables rarely follow it, so measured network distances are longer.

HTTP Strict Transport Security: a response header that tells a browser to use only HTTPS for a site for a set time (max-age). After seeing it, the browser upgrades http:// links itself, skipping an insecure request and its redirect.
example: Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000 asks the browser to remember the rule for a year.

definition: A list of domains built into browsers that must always be reached over HTTPS, so even the very first visit is protected. Site owners submit their domain to be added.

A store, in the browser or in a shared proxy, of earlier HTTP responses that can be reused while they are still fresh, as controlled by headers such as Cache-Control. A fresh hit needs no network traffic at all.
A connection that stays open after a response so later requests can reuse it, avoiding new TCP and TLS handshakes. HTTP/1.1 made this the default.
example: Fetching ten images over one persistent connection pays the handshakes once instead of ten times.

definition: Sending new requests over a connection that is already open (warm) instead of opening a new one. It skips DNS, TCP and TLS set-up and avoids restarting slow start.
A set of open connections kept ready by a client so requests can borrow one instead of opening a new connection each time.
example: An app keeps 20 open connections to its database and hands one to each query.

definition: The verb at the start of an HTTP request that says what the client wants to do, such as GET (read), POST (submit) or DELETE.
The HTTP method for reading a resource. It is defined as safe (it should not change server state), which makes it the usual choice for caching and for TLS early data.
example: GET /cart HTTP/1.1 asks the server for the cart page.

definition: The HTTP method for submitting data for the server to process, such as creating an order or a payment. It is not safe or idempotent by default, so repeating it can repeat its effect.

An HTTP method defined as read-only, such as GET, HEAD or OPTIONS: the client does not request any change on the server. RFC 8470 lets clients send only safe methods in TLS early data unless they know more.
A name–value line sent with an HTTP request or response that carries extra information, such as Host, Cookie or Cache-Control.
example: Accept-Encoding: gzip, br tells the server which compressions the client accepts.

definition: The HTTP/1.1 request header naming the hostname the client wants, so one server can host many sites. In HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 it becomes the :authority pseudo-header.
A special header in HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, written with a leading colon, that carries what HTTP/1.1 put in the request line or Host header: :method, :path, :scheme and :authority.
A small piece of data a server asks the browser to store (with Set-Cookie) and send back on later requests (in the Cookie header). It is commonly used to keep a user logged in.
example: Cookie: session=abc123 identifies the user's session to the server.

definition: The HTTP response header a server uses to ask the browser to store a cookie. A shared cache must not reuse a response that sets a user's cookie for other users.
The HTTP header that says what kind of data a body contains, such as text/html or application/json.
The HTTP header giving the size of the message body in bytes. It describes the body; it does not change how many round trips a request needs.
The request header listing which compression formats the client can decode, such as gzip and br (Brotli). Servers and CDNs use it to choose a compressed version.
The request header listing the languages the user prefers, with weights, for example fr-FR,fr;q=0.9,en;q=0.8. Raw values vary hugely, so CDNs usually normalise them before using them in a cache key.
The request header that identifies the client software, such as the browser name and version. There are thousands of distinct strings, so caching by the raw value fragments a cache badly.

The HTTP header that tells browsers and shared caches whether and for how long a response may be stored. Directives include max-age (seconds of freshness), private (browser only, not shared caches), no-store (never store) and immutable (won't change while fresh).
example: Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable lets a versioned asset be cached for a year.

definition: An HTTP response header that tells caches which request headers change the response, so they store a separate copy for each distinct value of those headers. Varying on a header with many values fragments the cache.
example: Vary: Accept-Encoding keeps gzip and Brotli copies apart.

definition: A response header carrying an identifier for a specific version of a resource. A cache can later ask whether its copy is still current (revalidation) and get a short 304 Not Modified reply instead of the full body.
A cache checking with the origin whether a stored response is still valid, usually with a conditional request using ETag or Last-Modified, instead of downloading it again.

A Cache-Control directive that lets a cache keep serving an expired copy for a set time while it fetches a fresh one in the background, so users don't wait and the origin gets one refresh instead of a burst.
example: Cache-Control: max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=30

definition: A three-digit number at the start of an HTTP response saying how the request went: 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.
example: 200 OK, 301 Moved Permanently, 404 Not Found, 503 Service Unavailable.

definition: A 3xx response telling the client to fetch a different URL instead. Redirecting http:// to https:// costs the client at least one extra round trip.
The HTTP status a server returns when the request itself is malformed. Like all 4xx codes, it blames the client, not the server.
The HTTP status a gateway or proxy (such as a CDN or load balancer) returns when it got an invalid response, or no usable response, from the server behind it.
The HTTP status a gateway or proxy returns when the server behind it did not answer in time.
The HTTP status meaning the server cannot handle the request right now, for example because it is overloaded or has no healthy backends.
A widely supported general-purpose compression format used to shrink HTTP responses such as HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
A compression format designed by Google, advertised as br in Accept-Encoding. It usually compresses web text smaller than gzip.
HyperText Markup Language: the text format of web pages. The browser parses it to build the page and to discover further resources to fetch.
Cascading Style Sheets: the language that describes how a web page looks (layout, colours, fonts). CSS files are static assets a browser fetches after the HTML.
The programming language that runs in web browsers (and in some servers and edge runtimes). Script files are among the resources a page loads.

A resource hint (<link rel="preconnect">) telling the browser to start DNS, TCP and TLS set-up to another origin early, before it discovers the actual request, so the handshake cost overlaps with other work.
The DNS response code meaning the queried name does not exist. Resolvers cache it for the zone's negative TTL.
example: dig no-such-name.example.com returns status NXDOMAIN.

definition: A system that allows or blocks network traffic according to rules. A firewall that silently drops packets makes connections hang until they time out, instead of failing at once.
A cloud virtual firewall (for example in AWS) attached to instances, listing which inbound and outbound traffic is allowed. Traffic it doesn't allow is dropped silently.
An access control list: ordered allow and deny rules for traffic. In AWS a network ACL applies to a whole subnet, alongside the security groups on individual instances.
A limit on how long a client waits for something (connecting, a response) before giving up. Without one, a silently dropped connection can hang for a long time.

The DNS server that does the work of a lookup for clients: it follows referrals from the root to the TLD to the authoritative server and caches every answer for its TTL. ISPs and public services such as 1.1.1.1 and 8.8.8.8 run them.
The small DNS client library in an operating system or app. It sends one recursive query to a configured resolver and waits for the final answer.

The servers at the top of the DNS hierarchy, which refer resolvers to the right top-level-domain servers. There are 13 named identities (a to m.root-servers.net) run by 12 organisations, each served by anycast from many sites.
The built-in list of root server names and addresses that a recursive resolver starts from when its cache is empty.
Top-level domain: the last label of a domain name, such as .com or .uk. TLD servers know which name servers are responsible for each domain registered under it.
example: For shop.example.com the TLD is .com.

definition: The DNS server that holds the actual records for a zone and gives definitive answers about it, rather than cached copies. Its operator decides what to answer, which is what makes DNS-based traffic steering possible.
Any server that answers DNS queries. A domain's NS records list the name servers that are authoritative for it.
A DNS reply that doesn't contain the answer but says which servers to ask next, for example a root server pointing a resolver at the .com servers.
A DNS query in which the server answers with what it knows, often a referral, and the asker follows the referrals itself. Recursive resolvers query root, TLD and authoritative servers this way.
A DNS query asking the server to return the final answer, doing any further lookups itself. Stub resolvers send recursive queries to recursive resolvers.
The portion of the DNS name space managed as one unit by one operator, such as example.com and the names under it, with its records held on its authoritative servers.
The name at the top of a DNS zone itself, such as example.com (not www.example.com). It must hold the zone's SOA and NS records, so it cannot be a CNAME.
A DNS record that maps a name to an IPv4 address.
example: api.example.com. 300 IN A 203.0.113.10

definition: A DNS record that maps a name to an IPv6 address.
example: api.example.com. AAAA 2001:db8::10

definition: A DNS record that makes one name an alias of another name, which the resolver then looks up. A name with a CNAME can't hold ordinary data, so the zone apex can't be a CNAME.
example: www.example.com CNAME shop.cdn.net sends lookups for www on to the CDN's name.

definition: A DNS record listing the authoritative name servers for a zone. Registrars publish them in the parent TLD zone to delegate a domain.
A DNS record naming the mail servers that accept email for a domain.
A DNS record holding free text, widely used for email policies such as SPF and for proving domain ownership to services.
A DNS record that gives the host and port for a named service, used for service discovery.
A DNS record listing which certificate authorities may issue certificates for a domain. Public CAs must check it before issuing.
example: example.com. CAA 0 issue "letsencrypt.org"

definition: The start-of-authority record at the top of every DNS zone. It holds administrative values for the zone, including the MINIMUM field used for negative caching.
The last numeric field of a zone's SOA record. RFC 2308 uses it to cap how long resolvers cache negative answers: the negative TTL is the smaller of it and the SOA record's own TTL.

A provider-specific DNS feature that lets the zone apex point at another hostname: the DNS provider resolves the target itself and returns ordinary A or AAAA records. Route 53 calls these alias records.
A newer DNS record type (RFC 9460) that tells clients up front how to connect to a service, for example that it supports HTTP/3 (alpn=h3), saving a round trip of discovery.
Caching the fact that a DNS name does not exist (NXDOMAIN), so repeated lookups for it don't hit the authoritative servers. RFC 2308 limits it to the smaller of the SOA TTL and the SOA MINIMUM field.

A resolver behaviour (RFC 8767) of answering from expired cache entries when the authoritative servers can't be reached, rather than failing. It cushions DNS outages but lets old answers outlive their TTL.
Extension Mechanisms for DNS: lets a DNS client advertise a UDP response size larger than the original 512 bytes, among other options. Around 1,232 bytes is the common safe default.
A coordinated 2020 change by DNS software vendors and operators to default to a 1,232-byte EDNS buffer size, avoiding IP fragmentation and using TCP for larger answers.
Splitting an IP packet that is too big for a link into smaller fragments that the receiver reassembles. Some middleboxes drop fragments, which can make large UDP DNS answers fail.
The truncated bit in a DNS response header. It tells the client the answer didn't fit in UDP and should be retried over TCP.
DNS Security Extensions: digital signatures on DNS records so resolvers can verify answers came from the zone owner and weren't altered. Signatures make responses larger.
DNS queries sent inside a TLS connection, normally on TCP port 853, so on-path observers can't read or alter them.
DNS queries sent as HTTPS requests, hiding them among ordinary web traffic. Browsers can use it instead of the operating system's resolver.
A company that registers domain names on behalf of their owners and publishes the domain's NS records into the TLD zone. It is not queried during ordinary resolution.
Returning several A records for one name and rotating their order, so clients spread across servers. It has no health awareness and reacts slowly because of caching.
Authoritative DNS that returns different answers depending on where the query appears to come from, usually by geolocating the resolver's (or, with ECS, the client's) IP address.
example: Return the eu-west-1 load balancer to European resolvers and us-east-1 to North American ones.

definition: A DNS extension that lets a recursive resolver pass a truncated part of the client's IP address (such as a /24) to authoritative servers, so geo-steering can use the user's location rather than the resolver's. It costs some privacy and cache efficiency.
AWS's managed DNS service. It offers routing policies such as weighted, latency-based, geolocation and health-checked failover.
Microsoft Azure's DNS-based traffic routing service, with methods such as priority (failover), weighted, performance and geographic.
A managed authoritative DNS provider (now part of IBM) known for traffic-steering features such as routing on real-user latency measurements.
A large CDN, DNS and security provider that serves its whole network from anycast addresses.

A DDoS attack on 21 October 2016 against the DNS provider Dyn, launched largely from the Mirai botnet of compromised devices. Sites that relied on Dyn, including Twitter, GitHub and Netflix, became unreachable for many users.
Distributed denial of service: flooding a target with traffic from many machines at once so it can't serve real users.
Announcing the same IP prefix from many locations so internet routing (BGP) delivers each packet to one of them, usually a nearby one by routing policy.
example: 1.1.1.1 and 8.8.8.8 are anycast addresses served from many sites worldwide.

definition: Ordinary one-to-one addressing, where an IP address belongs to a single destination.
Sending one packet to a group of receivers that have joined a group address. Anycast is different: each packet goes to exactly one location.
An open-source system that runs and manages containers across a cluster of machines: scheduling them, restarting them, and giving them networking and service discovery.
The smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes: one or more containers that share a network address and run together on one machine.
A Kubernetes object that gives a changing set of Pods one stable name and, normally, one stable virtual IP. Traffic to it is spread across the Pods behind it.
A Kubernetes Service with no virtual IP: its DNS name returns the individual Pod addresses instead, so client DNS caching affects which Pods get traffic.
An IP address that isn't tied to one machine but represents a service, with traffic to it forwarded to whichever backends are serving.
How a service finds the current network addresses of the services it calls, for example through DNS names or a registry, as instances come and go.
A regular automated probe, such as an HTTP request to /healthz, that decides whether a server or region should receive traffic.
Moving traffic or responsibility from a failed component (server, database, region) to a standby or other healthy one. Failing back returns it once the original recovers.
Sending a small share of traffic (say 5–10%) to a new version first and watching for problems before moving everyone over.
Splitting traffic between targets in set proportions, such as 90% to v1 and 10% to v2. With DNS, caching means actual request traffic only roughly follows the weights.
Sending each user to the region with the lowest measured latency for their network, rather than the geographically nearest one.
A building full of servers, storage and network equipment. A cloud region is made of several.
A block of IP addresses written as address/length, where the length says how many leading bits are fixed. A /24 IPv4 prefix holds 2^(32−24) = 256 addresses. BGP routes are announced for prefixes.
Java Virtual Machine: the runtime that executes Java (and Kotlin, Scala) programs. Older JVM configurations could cache DNS answers for much longer than their TTL.
The core software that manages a computer's hardware and runs programs, such as Linux, Windows, macOS, iOS or Android. It provides the network stack and the stub resolver.
Software development kit: a library and tools for using a platform or service from your code.
Request for Comments: the numbered document series that publishes internet standards and protocol specifications, such as RFC 9000 for QUIC.
Internet Engineering Task Force: the open standards body that develops internet protocols such as TCP, TLS, HTTP and QUIC, published as RFCs.
Sender Policy Framework: a TXT record listing which servers may send email for a domain, so receivers can spot forged senders.
Copying a DNS zone's records from one authoritative server to another, used to keep secondary servers or a second provider in sync.
An exchange of messages two parties make before the real communication starts, to set up a connection or agree keys. Each handshake costs at least one round trip.
How TCP opens a connection: the client sends SYN, the server replies SYN-ACK, the client sends ACK. Data can follow after one round trip.
The TCP segment a client sends to start a connection ('synchronise'). If SYNs are dropped silently, the client retries with growing gaps until its connect timeout.
The server's reply to a SYN, acknowledging it and sending its own SYN: the second step of the TCP three-way handshake.
An acknowledgement: a TCP (or QUIC) signal that data up to a point has arrived. Senders use ACKs to detect loss and to grow their congestion window.
A TCP segment that abruptly aborts a connection, for example when a host receives a packet for a connection it has no state for, or a SYN for a port nobody listens on.
The error a client gets when the target host answers a connection attempt with a reset because nothing is listening on that port. It arrives immediately, unlike a timeout.

A TCP extension (RFC 7413) that lets a returning client put data in its SYN using a cookie from an earlier connection, saving the handshake round trip. Deployment depends on both ends and middleboxes.
One unit of TCP data with its header, carried in one IP packet.
Maximum segment size: the most data a single TCP segment carries, typically 1,460 bytes on an Ethernet path (a 1,500-byte packet minus 40 bytes of IP and TCP headers).
Sending data again because the original was lost. TCP and QUIC detect loss from missing acknowledgements or timers.
A mechanism by which a receiver limits how much a sender may send, so it isn't overwhelmed. In TCP the receiver advertises a window of buffer space.
How a sender adjusts its sending rate to the capacity of the network path, probing for bandwidth and backing off when packets are lost.
The amount of unacknowledged data a sender allows itself in flight, set by congestion control. A new TCP connection commonly starts with 10 segments (about 14 KB, RFC 6928).

The phase at the start of a TCP (or QUIC) connection when the congestion window roughly doubles every round trip until loss appears, so new connections can't use a fast link fully at once. Load balancers also use the name for ramping traffic gradually to a newly added backend.
example: Starting at 14 KB, a 200 KB response needs about four round trips.

definition: A classic TCP congestion-control algorithm that halves its congestion window when it detects loss.
The default TCP congestion-control algorithm in Linux. On loss it cuts its window to about 70% (a cut of about 30%) and regrows along a cubic curve.
Packets that never arrive, because of congestion, faulty links or wireless interference. A few per cent is common on poor mobile or Wi-Fi links.
A self-contained packet of data sent without a connection, with no promise of delivery or order. UDP sends datagrams.
A protocol that sets up a connection with shared state before sending data, as TCP and QUIC do. Connectionless protocols such as UDP just send datagrams.

When one delayed item at the front of a queue holds up everything behind it. In HTTP/1.1 a slow response blocks later ones on the same connection; in TCP one lost packet holds back all later bytes, even for other HTTP/2 streams.
Where ordinary programs run, outside the operating-system kernel. QUIC is usually implemented in user space, so it can be updated with an app rather than an OS upgrade.

The text-based version of HTTP (first specified in 1997, now RFC 9112). It has persistent connections but handles one response at a time per connection, so browsers open about six connections per origin.
The 2015 version of HTTP (now RFC 9113). It keeps HTTP's meaning but sends binary frames and multiplexes many streams over one TCP connection, with HPACK header compression.
The version of HTTP that runs over QUIC instead of TCP (RFC 9114, 2022), avoiding TCP head-of-line blocking between streams.
Sending several HTTP/1.1 requests on one connection without waiting for each response. Responses still had to return in order and buggy proxies broke it, so browsers disabled it.
An HTTP/1.1-era trick of spreading assets over several hostnames (img1., img2.) to get more parallel connections. Under HTTP/2 it usually hurts.
An HTTP/1.1-era trick of combining many small images into one file (and many scripts or stylesheets into one, called concatenation) to cut the number of requests, at the cost of caching flexibility.
HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 split every message into small binary frames labelled with a stream ID, so frames from many requests can interleave on one connection.
One request–response exchange inside an HTTP/2 or QUIC connection, identified by a stream ID. Many streams share one connection.

Sharing one channel or resource among several independent streams or users, usually by interleaving them in time, and separating them again at the other end. HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests over one TCP connection.
HTTP/2's header-compression scheme (RFC 7541): repeated headers are sent as small references to a shared table. It assumes headers arrive in order.
HTTP/3's header compression (RFC 9204), redesigned from HPACK so out-of-order arrival over QUIC doesn't block unrelated streams.
The simple priority scheme for HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 (RFC 9218), using an urgency level and an incremental flag, which replaced HTTP/2's original dependency tree.
An HTTP/2 feature letting a server send responses the client hadn't asked for yet. It was hard to use well; Chrome removed support in 2022.
An informational HTTP response (RFC 8297) a server can send before the final response, telling the browser to start preloading or preconnecting to resources.
An HTTP response header (RFC 7838) advertising another way to reach the same service, typically h3=":443" to say HTTP/3 is available. The browser remembers it for ma seconds.
Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation: a TLS extension in which the client lists the protocols it speaks (such as h2 and http/1.1) and the server picks one during the handshake.
QUIC's ability to keep a connection alive when the client's IP address or port changes, for example moving from Wi-Fi to mobile data, because connections are identified by connection IDs.
An identifier carried in QUIC packets that names the connection independently of IP addresses and ports, enabling migration. Load balancers must route on it rather than the 4-tuple.
The four values that identify a connection: source IP, source port, destination IP and destination port.
The 4-tuple plus the protocol (such as TCP or UDP). L4 load balancers commonly hash it to pick a backend for a flow.
Network equipment between endpoints that inspects or changes traffic, such as firewalls, NATs and proxies. Middleboxes that assume old protocol behaviour make protocols hard to change.
When middleboxes come to depend on the details of a protocol's visible headers, so the protocol can no longer change. QUIC encrypts most of its headers to prevent it.
Generic Segmentation Offload: letting the kernel or network card split one large buffer into many packets, cutting per-packet CPU cost. It helps UDP-based QUIC.
IETF work on encoding routing information in server-chosen QUIC connection IDs so load balancers can keep sending a migrating connection to the same backend.
Datagram TLS: a version of TLS adapted to run over UDP datagrams, used by WebRTC and some games and VPNs.
A limit after which a server or pool closes a long-lived connection so clients reconnect, re-resolve DNS and spread across new backends. gRPC servers call it MAX_CONNECTION_AGE.
The client itself learns all backend addresses and spreads its requests across them, instead of going through a separate load balancer. gRPC supports it.
The time a link takes to put all of a message's bits onto the wire: size in bits divided by link rate. 200 KB at 1 Gbps takes 1.6 ms.
Wireless local networking based on the IEEE 802.11 standards. Wi-Fi links often see more packet loss and latency variation than wired ones.
A unit of data of 8 bits. Network rates are usually given in bits per second and sizes in bytes, so multiply bytes by 8 to compare.
1,000 bytes in this module (some contexts use 1,024 bytes, properly called a kibibyte, KiB).
10^9 bytes, a thousand megabytes.
10^15 bytes: a million gigabytes.
example: 2 million downloads of 40 GB is 80 PB.

definition: Gigabits per second: 10^9 bits per second, a measure of link speed. 1 Gbps moves about 125 megabytes per second.
Terabits per second: 10^12 bits per second.
One thousandth of a second, the usual unit for network latency.
A rate of incoming requests, the usual measure of load on a service.
A rate of packets handled, the usual capacity measure for L4 load balancers and routers.

The current version of TLS (RFC 8446, 2018). A full handshake needs one round trip, everything after the ServerHello is encrypted, and only forward-secret key exchanges are allowed for certificate handshakes.
The previous version of TLS (RFC 5246, 2008). A full handshake takes two round trips, and it still permits legacy options such as static RSA key exchange.
Server Name Indication: a TLS extension in which the client names the hostname it wants, so one IP address can serve many sites with different certificates. Without ECH it is sent unencrypted.

A TLS extension (RFC 9849, 2026) that encrypts most of the ClientHello, including the real SNI, inside an outer ClientHello that shows only a public name, so on-path observers can't see which site is being visited.
A signed document (in X.509 format) that binds a public key to one or more names, signed by a certificate authority. A server presents it to prove it is the site the client asked for.
An organisation trusted to issue certificates after checking that the requester controls the names in them. Browsers and operating systems ship a list of trusted root CAs.
A certificate authority whose self-signed certificate is in clients' trust stores. Chains of trust end at a root.
A CA certificate signed by a root (or another intermediate) that in turn signs leaf certificates. Servers must send their intermediates, or some clients can't build the chain.
The end-entity certificate for the actual server name, such as shop.example.com, at the bottom of a chain of trust.
The set of root CA certificates an operating system, browser or application trusts.
The sequence leaf → intermediate(s) → root, where each certificate is signed by the next. A client accepts a server's certificate only if it can build this chain to a root it trusts.
The certificate field listing every hostname (and possibly IP) the certificate is valid for.
A certificate for a name like *.example.com. The * matches exactly one leftmost label, so it covers shop.example.com but not eu.api.example.com or example.com itself.
A non-profit certificate authority that issues free, short-lived TLS certificates through the automated ACME protocol.
Automatic Certificate Management Environment (RFC 8555): the protocol software uses to prove domain control and obtain or renew certificates automatically.
The industry body of certificate authorities and browser makers that sets the baseline rules for publicly trusted certificates, including their maximum lifetime.
Public key infrastructure: the CAs, policies and tools that issue, manage and revoke certificates. A private PKI is one an organisation runs for its own internal services.
Declaring a certificate invalid before it expires, for example because its private key leaked, and telling clients through CRLs or OCSP.
Certificate revocation list: a signed list, published by a CA, of the serial numbers of certificates it has revoked.
Online Certificate Status Protocol: a client asks the CA whether one specific certificate is still valid. It adds a lookup and leaks browsing to the CA, and is now in decline.
The server fetches a fresh signed OCSP status for its own certificate and attaches ('staples') it to the TLS handshake, saving the client a lookup.
Compressed revocation lists that browsers push to themselves (Chrome's CRLSets, Firefox's CRLite), so they can check revocation without contacting CAs during the handshake.

A system of public, append-only logs that record issued certificates. Browsers require evidence of logging for publicly trusted certificates, and domain owners can monitor the logs for certificates they didn't request.
Authority Information Access: a certificate field with a URL where the issuer's certificate can be downloaded. Some browsers use it to fetch a missing intermediate; many other clients don't.
A named combination of cryptographic algorithms used for a TLS connection, such as the bulk encryption and hash. The client offers several and the server picks one.
The part of a handshake where two sides arrive at a shared secret key over an open network, without ever sending the key itself.

Ephemeral (elliptic-curve) Diffie–Hellman: a key exchange in which both sides send fresh public values each connection and each derives the same secret. Because the private values are thrown away, it gives forward secrecy.
In TLS 1.3, the public value a side sends for a particular key-exchange group. The client sends its share in the first message, which is what makes a 1-RTT handshake possible.
The specific curve or algorithm used for a key exchange, such as X25519. If the server doesn't support the group the client guessed, a HelloRetryRequest costs an extra round trip.
A widely used elliptic-curve Diffie–Hellman key-exchange function (RFC 7748), a common first guess in TLS 1.3 ClientHellos.

A TLS key exchange that combines a classical method (such as X25519) with one designed to resist future quantum computers (such as ML-KEM), so the result stays secure if either holds. Browsers and CDNs have begun offering it.
The first TLS handshake message, from client to server, listing supported versions, cipher suites, a key share, SNI and ALPN. Without ECH it is unencrypted.
The server's first TLS handshake message: its chosen parameters and its own key share. In TLS 1.3 everything after it is encrypted.
A TLS 1.3 handshake message, sent encrypted right after ServerHello, carrying extension responses that don't need to be in the clear (such as the chosen ALPN protocol).
The TLS handshake message in which the server signs the handshake transcript with its certificate's private key, proving it holds that key.
The last TLS handshake message from each side: a check value over the whole handshake, confirming nobody tampered with it.
A TLS 1.3 reply asking the client to send a new ClientHello with a key share for a different group, costing an extra round trip.
The record of all handshake messages exchanged so far, which CertificateVerify signs and Finished checks.
The property that stealing a server's long-term private key later does not let an attacker decrypt traffic recorded earlier, because each session used fresh ephemeral keys.
A key generated for a single session and then discarded.
Pre-shared key: a secret both sides already hold. In TLS 1.3, resumption and 0-RTT use a PSK derived from an earlier handshake.
Reconnecting with a key from an earlier TLS session (a PSK from a session ticket) instead of a full certificate handshake. It saves CPU and bytes; without 0-RTT it still takes one round trip.
Data a server gives a client so it can resume the session later. Stateless tickets are encrypted with a server ticket key, so every server that should accept them needs that key.

TLS 1.3 (and QUIC) resumption in which the client sends its request in its very first flight, saving a round trip. Early data can be replayed by an attacker and lacks some forward-secrecy protections.
An attacker capturing a valid message and sending it again so its effect happens twice, such as a payment request. TLS early data is vulnerable to replay across connections.
Whether a request can be processed more than once without harm. Servers must check this before accepting it as TLS early data.
A request header (RFC 8470) that a proxy adds when it forwards a request that arrived in TLS early data, so the origin can refuse it with 425 Too Early.
The HTTP status an origin returns to refuse a request received as TLS early data; the client then retries after the handshake completes.
A TLS 1.2 optimisation (RFC 7918) letting the client send application data before the handshake fully completes, saving a round trip.
A legacy TLS key exchange in which the client encrypts the session secret with the server's long-term RSA key. It has no forward secrecy and was removed in TLS 1.3.
Cipher block chaining: an older block-cipher mode. CBC cipher suites in TLS suffered padding attacks and were dropped in TLS 1.3.
An old cryptographic hash function now broken for collision resistance, so it is no longer allowed for certificate signatures or in TLS 1.3.
A widely used cryptographic hash function from the SHA-2 family, producing a 256-bit digest.
Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm. For similar security, ECDSA keys and signatures are much smaller than RSA ones, which keeps certificate chains small.
A standard elliptic curve (NIST P-256) commonly used for ECDSA certificate keys, giving roughly the security of RSA-3072 with 256-bit keys.
RSA keys of 2,048 or 4,096 bits. Bigger keys mean bigger certificates and much slower signing.
Public-key cryptography based on the maths of elliptic curves, which gets strong security from small keys.
A TLS extension (RFC 8879) that compresses the certificate chain in the handshake when both sides support it, helping it fit in TCP's initial window.
The point where an encrypted TLS connection ends and the traffic is decrypted, such as a load balancer or CDN edge.
Decrypting TLS at the outer edge of your system (a CDN or load balancer) and sending plain traffic inside. Simple, but the internal hop is unencrypted.
Terminating TLS at a load balancer to inspect the request, then opening a new TLS connection to the backend so the internal hop is encrypted too.
A load balancer forwarding encrypted TLS connections to backends without decrypting them. It can route by SNI but can't see paths or headers.
A security model that grants no automatic trust to anything inside the network: every connection is authenticated, authorised and encrypted.
An attacker who has broken into one machine moving on to others inside the same network.
TLS in which the client also presents a certificate, so both sides prove their identity. Service meshes use it between services.

Request headers proxies add so the app can learn the original client: X-Forwarded-For lists client and proxy IPs (each proxy appends one), X-Forwarded-Proto says whether the client used HTTPS. Forwarded (RFC 7239) is the standard form. Clients can forge them, so trust only entries added by your own proxies.
Web application firewall: filters HTTP requests for attacks such as SQL injection before they reach the application.
A TLS extension (RFC 9345) letting a server operator issue short-lived signing keys to, for example, a CDN, so the CDN never holds the certificate's long-term private key.
A command-line tool for making HTTP and other requests. Unlike desktop browsers it doesn't fetch missing intermediate certificates, so it exposes broken chains.
Internet of Things: networked devices such as sensors, meters and cameras, often with a certificate installed at manufacture.
Business-to-business: services one company provides to another, such as partner APIs.
A popular open-source service mesh for Kubernetes, with Envoy-based sidecar or ambient data planes and the istiod control plane.
An open-source service mesh for Kubernetes that provides mTLS, retries and metrics with its own lightweight proxy.
Secure Production Identity Framework for Everyone: a standard for giving each workload a verifiable identity (a SPIFFE ID such as spiffe://example.org/payments) carried in short-lived certificates.
The reference implementation of SPIFFE: it verifies workloads and issues and rotates their identity certificates.
The security property that only intended parties can read data. TLS provides it by encrypting traffic.
Layer 4, the transport layer (TCP, UDP) in the OSI model. An L4 load balancer chooses a backend per connection or flow from IP addresses and ports, without reading HTTP.
Layer 7, the application layer (HTTP, gRPC) in the OSI model. An L7 load balancer terminates the connection, parses requests and can route each one by path, header or cookie.
A seven-layer reference model of networking, from physical (1) to application (7). People use its numbers loosely: L4 for transport, L7 for application.
Short for load balancer: a component that spreads incoming connections or requests across a pool of servers.
Amazon Web Services, Amazon's cloud platform.
AWS Network Load Balancer: a managed L4 (TCP/UDP/TLS) load balancer.
AWS Application Load Balancer: a managed L7 (HTTP/HTTPS, gRPC) load balancer with path and header routing.
Google's software L4 load balancer (NSDI 2016). Its Maglev hashing builds a lookup table that spreads connections almost evenly and moves few of them when backends change.
Meta's open-source L4 load balancer, which forwards packets in the Linux kernel using XDP and eBPF for very high packet rates.
An open-source L4/L7 proxy widely used as a load balancer, API gateway and service-mesh sidecar.
A widely used web server and reverse proxy, often placed in front of application servers for TLS, buffering, caching and load balancing.
A widely used open-source TCP and HTTP load balancer and proxy.
An open-source web server and reverse proxy known for obtaining TLS certificates automatically.
An open-source reverse proxy and load balancer that configures itself from container platforms such as Kubernetes.
A lightweight publish/subscribe messaging protocol over TCP, common for IoT devices.
Simple Mail Transfer Protocol: the protocol mail servers use to send email to each other.
An L4 load-balancing mode in which backends send responses straight to clients, using the service IP as source, so only the (usually small) inbound traffic passes through the balancer.
Equal-cost multi-path routing: a router spreads flows across several equally good next hops, often by hashing the 5-tuple. It is used to spread traffic over a fleet of L4 balancers.
Taking turns: sending each new request (or task) to the next server in a fixed rotation. Fair only if every request costs the same and servers are identical.
Round robin in which each server gets a share of turns proportional to its weight, so bigger servers get more traffic.
Load-balancing algorithms that send each new request to the backend with the fewest open connections or in-flight requests, so slow servers naturally receive less.
Pick two backends at random and send the request to the less loaded one. It gets almost all the benefit of full least-loaded selection with little coordination, and avoids herding.
Many independent balancers all choosing the same apparently least-loaded backend at once and overloading it.
The remainder after whole-number division, written a mod b or a % b. 23 mod 10 = 3.
Assigning a key to server hash(key) mod N. Simple and even, but changing the number of servers N moves almost every key.
The circle of hash values used by consistent hashing: servers and keys are placed on it, and each key belongs to the next server clockwise.
Many points on a consistent-hashing ring for each real server (often 100–200), which evens out load and spreads a failed server's keys across all survivors.
Highest-random-weight hashing: for each key, score every server with hash(key, server) and pick the highest. Adding or removing a server moves only the keys it wins or loses.

Sending work back to the place whose cache already holds its data. In load balancing it means routing the same key (such as a user ID) to the same server so it finds that user's data already cached there; operating systems use the same idea to keep a thread on the CPU core whose caches are warm.
A load balancer probing each backend on a schedule (for example GET /healthz every 10 s) and marking it unhealthy after several failures in a row.
Passive health checking: watching real traffic and temporarily ejecting a backend that returns errors, such as 5 consecutive 5xx responses (Envoy's default).
A URL such as /healthz that a service exposes for health checks. What it checks decides whether failures cascade.

Fail open: when too many backends look unhealthy, keep sending traffic to all of them rather than none. Fail closed: refuse traffic instead. Which is better depends on whether some errors beat a total outage.
Envoy's fail-open rule: if the healthy share of hosts drops below the threshold (50% by default), it balances across all hosts as if they were healthy.
A Kubernetes check that decides whether a container is stuck and should be restarted.
A Kubernetes check that decides whether a container should receive traffic right now. Failing it removes the Pod from load balancing without restarting it.
Stopping new requests to a server being removed while letting in-flight ones finish.
AWS's name for connection draining on a target group: how long the load balancer waits for in-flight requests before removing a target. Default 300 s, range 0–3,600 s.
Routing all of a client's requests to the same backend, using a cookie or a hash of the client IP.
A shared place, such as Redis or a database, where per-user session data lives, so any server can handle any request.
Linux software that uses VRRP to move a floating IP between a pair of machines, giving active/passive failover for load balancers.
Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (RFC 5798): lets a backup machine take over a shared IP address when the active one fails.
An IP address that can be moved from one machine to another, so clients keep the same address after a failover.
A redundancy setup in which one site or machine serves while a standby waits to take over.
A redundancy setup in which every site or machine serves traffic all the time, so failover means shifting load to ones already running.
A set of components that can fail together because of a shared dependency, such as one rack, zone or region.
Preparing capacity or caches before traffic arrives, such as asking a provider to scale a load balancer before a launch, or loading content into CDN caches before a release.
Sending realistic, high volumes of synthetic traffic to a system to find its limits before real users do.
A managed group of identical instances whose size the cloud adjusts automatically between a minimum and maximum. New instances take minutes to start.
Many clients or processes all acting at the same moment, for example reconnecting together or all missing a cache together, and overwhelming a shared resource.
Waiting longer after each failed attempt, typically doubling a base delay each time, with a random component (jitter) so many clients don't retry in lockstep.
example: With full jitter, the wait before attempt k is a random time between 0 and base × 2^k.

definition: Network interface card: the hardware that connects a machine to the network.
A copy of a database that serves read queries, kept up to date from the primary.
A queue where slow work is placed to be processed later by background workers, so web requests return quickly.
A proxy that acts for clients, such as a corporate web proxy: websites see the proxy's address, not the user's.
Traffic entering or leaving your system, between external clients and your services.
Traffic between services inside your system.
A reverse proxy specialised for APIs used by external clients. It handles cross-cutting concerns such as authentication, rate limits, routing to many services and transformation.
Infrastructure that handles service-to-service traffic (mTLS, retries, timeouts, load balancing, metrics) through proxies managed by a control plane, without changing application code.
A proxy deployed next to each service instance (in the same Pod) that intercepts its inbound and outbound traffic.
The part of a system that handles live traffic, such as proxies forwarding requests, routers forwarding packets or DNS servers answering queries. It is kept simple and highly available.
The part of a system that configures the data plane: APIs, consoles and controllers that create resources and push rules and certificates. It is more complex and can be unavailable during incidents.
A reverse proxy reading a whole response (or request) into memory or temporary files, so the app worker is freed quickly while the proxy deals with a slow client. It delays streamed responses.
A response header an app can send to NGINX (X-Accel-Buffering: no) to turn off proxy buffering for that response, for example for streams.
A Python WSGI application server that runs a fixed number of worker processes; usually placed behind NGINX.
A Ruby application server, commonly used with Rails behind a reverse proxy.
An app-server process that handles one request at a time from start to finish, so it is occupied for as long as the client takes.
A single thread that waits for many network events at once and handles each as it becomes ready, so one process can serve thousands of slow connections cheaply.
An explicit list of permitted items, with everything else rejected or ignored.
A secret string a client sends with API requests to identify its account, used for access control, quotas and billing.
A limit on how much of a resource a user or customer may consume in a period, such as 1,000 API requests per minute on a free plan. Gateways and rate limiters enforce API quotas per key or account.
AWS's managed API gateway service.
An open-source API gateway built on NGINX.
Google Cloud's API management platform.
Microsoft Azure's API gateway and management service.
A separate gateway or thin service per client type (mobile, web) that aggregates and shapes data for that client, for example turning six calls into one round trip.
A need shared by many parts of a system, such as authentication, logging or rate limiting, as opposed to one service's own business logic.
The rules specific to what an application does, such as pricing or who may see an order, as opposed to generic infrastructure.

A Netflix Java library (now in maintenance) for timeouts, circuit breakers and fallbacks in service-to-service calls; with the Ribbon client load balancer it exemplified the 'library in every service' approach.
Istio's control plane, which issues certificates and pushes routing and policy configuration to the proxies.
Releasing a change to a growing share of traffic (canaries, percentage rollouts, header routing) while watching metrics, rather than to everyone at once.
How well you can understand a system's internal behaviour from its outputs: metrics, logs and traces.
Data that systems emit about their own behaviour, such as request rates, errors, latency and traces.
Following one request across every service it touches by passing a trace ID with each call and recording a timed span for each step.
One timed operation within a distributed trace, such as one service call.
The W3C Trace Context request header carrying a trace ID and parent span ID between services. Apps must copy incoming context into outgoing calls for spans to link up.
An open-source standard and set of libraries for producing metrics, logs and traces.
Google SRE's four key service metrics: latency, traffic, errors and saturation.
An Istio data-plane mode without per-Pod sidecars: a per-node ztunnel proxy handles L4 and mTLS, and optional waypoint proxies handle L7 features.
Istio ambient mode's per-node L4 proxy, which provides mTLS and identity for all Pods on its node.
An optional shared L7 proxy in Istio ambient mode, deployed only where HTTP features such as retries or header routing are needed.
A service-mesh mode in which gRPC client libraries receive mesh configuration directly (via xDS) instead of going through a sidecar proxy.
A proxy at the edge of a cluster or mesh that receives external traffic and routes it to internal services.
Automatically repeating a failed request. Safe only for idempotent requests, and dangerous when several layers retry.
Retries multiplying across layers or clients until they swamp an already struggling service, turning overload into outage.

A cap on retries as a fraction of normal traffic (say 10–20%), so retries help with blips but can't multiply load during a real failure. Envoy's version, for example, limits concurrent retries to 20% of active requests by default.
Passing a request's absolute deadline along to every downstream call, so inner services stop working once the caller has given up. gRPC supports it.
A long-established caching proxy server, often deployed as a forward proxy by companies and schools.
A standard way for a server to stream a series of text events to a browser over one long-lived HTTP response.
Code that runs one query to get a list and then one more query per item, so one page causes N+1 database round trips.
A CDN server near users that answers requests from its cache or forwards them towards the origin.
A CDN or network site, usually in a city's data centre, holding edge servers. Often abbreviated PoP.
Your own server that holds the original content, which a CDN or proxy fetches from on a cache miss. Usually just called the origin.
The usual CDN model: an edge fetches content from the origin the first time it is requested (a miss) and caches it.
A CDN model in which you upload or pre-position content on the CDN before anyone requests it, suiting large, predictable files.
A request answered from a cache's stored copy without going to the original source.
A request the cache can't answer from its stored copies, so it must fetch from the original source.
The fraction of requests served from cache. The origin's load is set by the miss fraction, so 95% to 99% hits cuts origin traffic five-fold.
The set of request properties (host, path, chosen query parameters, headers, cookies) that decides which requests share one cached object.
A cache key that includes values which don't change the response (tracking parameters, raw user agents), so one popular object is split into many rarely hit copies.
The part of a URL after ?, holding name=value parameters separated by &.
example: In /p/42?sort=price&page=2 the query string is sort=price&page=2.

definition: Marketing tracking query parameters (utm_source, utm_campaign and so on) that analytics tools read; they don't change the page.
Unique tracking parameters that Facebook (fbclid) and Google Ads (gclid) add to links, giving almost every visit a different URL.
An attack that tricks a cache into storing a victim's private page under a static-looking URL (such as /account/x.css) so the attacker can then fetch it.
Telling a CDN to drop cached objects, by URL, prefix or tag, so the next request fetches fresh content. Purging everything at once causes a miss storm.
Putting a version or content hash in an asset's file name (app.3f9a1c.js) so new content always has a new URL; old copies can then be cached for a year and never need purging.
A short fingerprint computed from a file's bytes, so any change to the file changes the hash.
A label attached to cached responses, such as product-42, so one purge call can remove every object with that tag across many URLs.
Arranging CDN caches in layers: edge PoPs ask a regional or shield tier on a miss, which alone talks to the origin.
A designated CDN cache that all edges go through on a miss, so many edge misses become one origin request. Best placed near the origin.
When many requests for the same uncached object arrive together, sending one request upstream and serving all of them from its response.
A browser reusing one HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 connection for several hostnames when they resolve to the same IP and one certificate covers them all.
A sudden flood of cache misses, for example after purging everything, that sends most traffic to the origin at once.
CDN techniques that speed up uncacheable requests: terminating TCP and TLS near the user, keeping warm connections to the origin and using better routes.
A provider's own long-distance network between its sites, often faster and less lossy than public internet routes.
Running your code on CDN edge servers near users, for redirects, A/B tests or auth checks. Fast only if the data it needs is also nearby.
Cloudflare's platform for running JavaScript and WebAssembly at its edge locations.
Fastly's edge compute platform, which runs WebAssembly at its PoPs.
Lightweight JavaScript functions that run at Amazon CloudFront edge locations for simple request and response changes.
AWS Lambda functions run in CloudFront's regional edge locations, for heavier request and response processing.
A database that stores values under unique keys and looks them up by key.
Showing two versions to different groups of users at random and comparing results.
Using more than one CDN provider, with DNS or other steering between them, so one provider's outage doesn't take the site down.
One of the oldest and largest CDN providers, classically steering users to PoPs through DNS.
A CDN and edge-cloud provider. A configuration change triggering a latent bug caused a widespread outage of its network in June 2021.
AWS's CDN service.
Google Cloud's CDN, served from Google's edge network behind its global load balancer.
Netflix's own CDN: appliances placed inside ISPs and exchange points, filled with predicted popular content during off-peak hours.
Internet service provider: a company that connects homes, offices or mobile users to the internet.
Traffic leaving a network, data centre or cloud. Clouds usually charge for egress bandwidth.
An HTTP request for only part of a file (using the Range header), used to resume or parallelise large downloads.
Short codes AWS uses for its regions: us-east-1 is Northern Virginia, eu-west-1 is Ireland and ap-southeast-1 is Singapore.
A geographic area where a cloud provider runs a cluster of data centres, such as Northern Virginia or Frankfurt. Multi-region systems run in several.
Deciding which region each user talks to and moving traffic when regions fail, using DNS steering, anycast or edge routing.
A requirement that certain data be stored or processed only in specific countries or regions, such as EU users' data in the EU.
Estimating where a device is from its IP address using databases. It is approximate and is fooled by VPNs, proxies and distant resolvers.
Virtual private network: an encrypted tunnel carrying a device's traffic to another network, so websites see the VPN's address and location.
Measuring performance as experienced by real users, typically with JavaScript in their browsers that reports timings back (beacons).
A network (or group of networks) under one operator with its own routing policy and number, such as an ISP or cloud provider. BGP routes between autonomous systems.
The list of autonomous systems a BGP route passes through. After local policy, BGP prefers the shortest one.
Adding your own AS number to a route announcement several times to make the path look longer, nudging other networks to prefer another route.
A BGP attribute a network sets for its own routing policy; the highest wins before path length is considered. It usually encodes customers over peers over paid transit.
Multi-exit discriminator: a BGP attribute a neighbour network uses to hint which of several links it prefers you to use, compared after local preference and AS path.
Interior gateway protocol: routing within one network, such as OSPF or IS-IS. BGP can use the IGP cost to the exit point as a late tie-breaker.
Two networks connecting directly to exchange traffic between their customers, usually without payment.
Paying a larger network to carry your traffic to the rest of the internet.
The period after a route change while routers across the internet exchange updates and settle on new paths: often seconds, sometimes a minute or more.
A BGP message saying a network no longer offers a route to a prefix, so others switch to their next-best route.
Tags attached to BGP routes that ask neighbouring networks to treat them a certain way, such as not announcing them further.
The set of users or networks whose traffic routing sends to a particular anycast site.
An AWS service giving you static anycast IP addresses that bring users onto AWS's network at the nearest edge and route them over its backbone to healthy endpoints.
Supporting both IPv4 and IPv6 at the same time.
Copying writes to a replica after acknowledging them to the client. Fast, but writes not yet copied are lost if the primary is destroyed.
Acknowledging a write only once it is durably stored on one or more replicas too. No acknowledged write is lost if the primary dies, at the cost of extra latency.
How far a replica is behind its primary, in time or in un-applied writes.
Recovery point objective: the maximum acceptable amount of data loss after a disaster, expressed as a time window.
example: An RPO of 5 minutes means losing at most the last 5 minutes of writes is acceptable.

definition: Using different thresholds or delays for switching one way and switching back, so a value hovering near a threshold doesn't flip back and forth.
A state repeatedly switching back and forth, such as a marginal region alternating between healthy and unhealthy and traffic bouncing between regions.
A location from which a health check or measurement is made. Checking from several prevents one network blip from looking like an outage.
Deliberately moving all traffic out of a region, as practice or during an incident.
Two parts of a system each believing they are the primary and accepting conflicting writes, usually after losing contact with each other.
Blocking a node that may wrongly think it is still primary from making changes, for example by having storage reject writes with an old token.
Deliberately rejecting or degrading some requests when overloaded, so the rest are served well instead of everything failing.
The margin between normal operating level and the maximum a system can handle, kept in reserve for spikes or failures.

How much of a resource's capacity is in use, usually as a percentage; at 100% it can accept no more work without queueing. In capacity planning it is measured against what each region or server can handle.
A cache that is empty or holds little useful data (cold) and so misses often, as opposed to a warm cache already full of popular items.
How easy a system is to run in production: deploying, scaling, replacing and debugging it.
